quote: And again, the priests are written down as more eminent than the Levites. For thus it is contained in the same Scripture: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take the sum of the Levites, and set them in the sight of Aaron the priest, and let them minister to him." You see in this too how it names the priests as superior to the Levites, and again sets the Levites as more eminent than the children of Israel?

quote: But also what it says — "in place of every firstborn that opens the womb" — does not seem to me able to be easily discussed or explained. For not everyone who opens the womb is straightway to be held worthy of the sanctification of the firstborn, since we also read in the Psalms that: "The sinners are estranged from the womb, they have gone astray from the belly, they have spoken false things." Which certainly can in no way stand according to the letter. For how could anyone go astray from the way of God the moment he came forth from his mother's belly? Or how could a child just brought forth speak false things or utter any sort of speech at all? Since therefore it is impossible either for anyone to go astray from the belly or to speak false things, it will be necessary that such a belly and womb be sought to which this saying can fit, that: "The sinners are estranged from the womb and…

"And the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses, saying: Behold, I have taken the Levites from the midst of the sons of Israel, in place of every firstborn that opens the womb from among the sons of Israel; they shall be their redemption, and the Levites shall be mine. For every firstborn is mine. From the day when I struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I sanctified to myself every firstborn of Israel; from man even to beast it shall be mine; I am the Lord." The Levites are taken in place of the firstborn, though indeed they are not firstborn. For Levi is born third from Leah; for first is Reuben, second Simeon, third Levi; and these are taken as firstborn who by nature are not firstborn. Is it to be believed that these things are written in the law of God without purpose? Or does it teach us this: that with God those are not reckoned firstborn who come first by bodily birth, but those…

But, if it seems good, let us return once more to the very order of the history that is recounted in Numbers, and from it let us contemplate where and how the mystery of the firstborn ought to be sought. Let us therefore review more attentively how the twelve tribes are distributed by threes into four parts and settle in a fixed station at each of the quarters of the heavens, and we find Judah indeed stationed on the east with Issachar and Zebulun, but Reuben on the west with Simeon and Gad; on the south Ephraim with Benjamin and Manasseh, but on the north Dan with Naphtali and Asher. Out of all these, placed as it were around the four corners of the earth in a circuit, in the midst of them, as being nearest to God, around the very tabernacle of God, the Levites are stationed. After these things, when the sons of Levi had been divided into three orders, and each of the orders was reckoned according to the three names of the princes, certain diversities are recorded in them too, not without mysteries. For the order of the sons of Kohath is described first, and rightly; for from him descend Moses and Aaron, to whom the summit of the priesthood is committed. For from him is born Amram; and from Amram, Moses and Aaron. The second order is Gershon, who indeed is first in birth, but is held second in order; for thus the Scripture says: "And the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari." But from the sons of Kohath again two orders are directed, and those indeed who descend from Aaron are consigned to the priesthood, while the remaining part is ordained to minister to the priests; and therefore the offices of the Levites are divided into four parts, so that Aaron…

It is the book of Numbers that is read to us, in which there are many differences of numbers, which are recorded concerning the sons of Israel. But after the sons of Israel, the Levites too are numbered separately. For they had not been counted along with the sons of Israel, and they have a certain number set apart and distinguished above the rest, by which they are all together reported to be found twenty-two thousand, so that neither anything more nor less than this was found in the number. After this the Lord commanded that the firstborn of the sons of Israel also be numbered in the same order in which the Levites had been numbered, that is, from one month and upward, and the firstborn of the sons of Israel are found to be twenty-two thousand and two hundred and seventy-three.
